data.title: Trump envoys set for Zelensky meeting after Russia-Ukraine peace talks with Putin
data.description:
President Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff on Sunday made their way to Kyiv to discuss the Ukraine war with the country’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky.

The New York Times reported that Witkoff and Kushner made it to the Ukrainian capital by train and later traveled via motorcade to meet Zelensky. Both CNN and the Times reported that their arrival followed discussion with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.

Witkoff and Kushner were set to travel to Russia and Ukraine this weekend, per previous reports, in an attempt to relaunch peace talks between the two countries. The war between Russia and Ukraine will reach the four-year mark next February if it does not conclude before then.

Zelensky said that he and his own negotiating team had met prior to discussions with Witkoff and Kushner, according to CNN.

“We are ready for talks. Ukraine has always been and will continue to be constructive,” Zelensky said on Telegram, per CNN.

Zelensky posted a video of himself hugging both Witkoff and Kushner on the social platform X Sunday morning. The Ukrainian leader said that the two sides “began talks,” in the caption.

Last Tuesday, Zelensky advised airlines against entering Russian airspace as his military responded to an “escalation” in missile and drone attacks.

The Ukrainian president said in an address that Russia had recently switched up its defense tactics, turning toward strikes from Ukrainian airspace. In the wake of a wave of attacks, Zelensky said that type of warfare “cannot and will not remain confined” to his country’s territory.

data.title: Live updates: Energy secretary set for Sunday show interviews as US, Iran trade strikes
data.description:
Energy Secretary Chris Wright is appearing on four Sunday morning news programs after the U.S. and Iran traded tit-for-tat strikes this weekend.

Iranian officials on Sunday took credit for an attack on an unmanned U.S. military ship in the Strait of Hormuz. That strike came after the U.S. hit three Iranian crude oil carriers in response to “multiple unprovoked” attacks by Iran on two U.S. Navy warships.

Oil prices jumped earlier this week amid earlier renewed strikes by the two countries. The price of Brent crude oil, the international benchmark, hit $96.28 per barrel on Friday.

Wright is also making appearances as controversy swirls around the Trump administration’s Venezuela oil deal. Hill Insiders can read more here.

Elsewhere, the GOP is gearing up for the Republican National Committee’s first-of-its-kind midterm convention in Texas this week, but some are already looking two years ahead. Here’s where the potential Republican 2028 presidential election contenders stand.

President Trump is at his golf club in Bedminster, N.J., with no public events scheduled as of Sunday morning.

Follow live below.

data.title: Iran attacks US ship in Strait of Hormuz
data.description:
Iran has said that it attacked an American ship in the Strait of Hormuz, according to state media.

Iranian state-run media outlet Press TV reported Sunday that a U.S. military vessel, which was remotely-operated, had been attacked by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), according to the military group itself.

Per an IRGC statement, the vessel had been trying to go into a restricted portion in the Strait of Hormuz, Press TV reported.

“With the grace and favor of Almighty God, every desperate move by the enemy is being closely monitored by brave, self-sacrificing IRGC Navy forces and will be met with a decisive attack,” the IRGC said in its Sunday statement, per Press TV.

On Saturday, U.S. Central Command (Centcom) conducted strikes on multiple Iranian crude oil carriers due to “multiple unprovoked” attacks from Iran on two American warships, per the military command.

U.S. forces “permanently disabled” three IRGC crude oil carriers near Kharg Island and in the Gulf of Oman. There were no U.S. service members harmed in the Iranian attacks, Centcom said.

“Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost —taking out three of yours,” Centcom Commander Adm. Brad Cooper said in a statement shared on social media. “We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet.”

Both the U.S. and Iran ramped up their military operations last week. On Tuesday, the U.S. carried out about 100 strikes against Iranian targets, and Tehran responded, targeting U.S. military bases and allies via strikes across the Middle East.

data.title: Trump is waging a war on America's children — and he's winning
data.description:
President Trump’s administration is waging war against children, especially those in our nation’s poorest families. Here are a few of the fronts on which that undeclared war is being fought, with devastating consequences for the next generation of Americans. 

Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act made massive cuts to Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program or SNAP, leaving millions of children in low-income families without access to health insurance, adequate and healthy food and, in some cases, learning and developmental services in public schools.  

Roughly 40 percent of American children receive health coverage through Medicaid. Although the bill’s work requirements do not apply to children, they lose coverage when their parents do. The Congressional Budget Office estimates the cuts will increase the number of Americans without health insurance by 7.5 million in 2034.

The budget office also projects that SNAP spending will decline by $211 billion through 2035. An analysis by the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities estimates 1.5 million children, conservatively, have lost benefits since July 2025. Further reductions are likely as states are forced to pay a larger share of the program’s administrative costs.  

The 2025 bill did increase the Child Tax Credit from $2,000 to $2,200. But it left intact rules that prevent many low-income families from receiving the full credit. As a result, 30 percent of all children and 99 percent of those from the poorest one-fifth of families won’t benefit from the increase.

Each of these individual policies is onerous, but the collective impact is especially damaging, since many families will be hurt by all of them.

The Trump administration’s vaccine policies have put children at risk as well. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and his handpicked appointees have promoted vaccine skepticism, parental choice and limits to state requirements that children be vaccinated before they start school. They claim, without evidence, that COVID-19 vaccines have killed children and that vaccines cause autism.

As a result, vaccination rates are falling. The share of kindergartners exempted from one or more required vaccines has increased from 2.2 percent in 2020-2021 to 4.2 percent in 2025. Only 92 percent of kindergarten students now get the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, well below the 95 percent needed for herd immunity. 

The consequences are not hypothetical. Americans have experienced the largest measles outbreak in three decades, with the vast majority of cases among unvaccinated children. 

Yet Trump’s Aug. 10 executive order pares back the number of recommended childhood vaccines and calls for splitting the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three separately administered shots — changes strongly opposed by mainstream medical organizations because they will leave many more children vulnerable to preventable diseases. 

That same month, the Trump administration proposed deregulating Head Start, one of the country’s most important programs for poor children. Head Start provides preschool, child care, meals and support services to about 700,000 children, many of them homeless, in foster care or disabled. The administration has already closed half of Head Start’s regional offices. Now it intends to reduce the federal overhead payments from 15 percent to 5 percent and eliminate or dilute national standards governing student-teacher ratios, educational requirements, medical screenings, program hours and other services.

The administration claims these changes will reduce costs and allow Head Start to serve more children. But this approach removes requirements intended to bolster program quality. Project 2025, it is worth noting, advocated eliminating Head Start. The administration’s approach will, at a minimum, dramatically reduce its effectiveness.

Meanwhile, tens of thousands of children whose parents have been arrested, detained or deported, or fear they will be, are suffering serious and lasting effects. Faced with economic instability, loss of housing, absence from school, fewer doctor visits, and sometimes foster care, they experience separation anxiety, headaches, stomach aches, difficulty sleeping and eating, and anxiety and depression.

More than 12,000 children and their parents or sponsors have been arrested following tips from the federal Office of Refugee Resettlement, an office that previously maintained a sharp separation between child-welfare responsibilities and immigration enforcement so parents would not be prevented from reuniting with their children. 

Trump’s war on children doesn’t stop at America’s borders. Researchers estimate that reductions in health care, nutrition, clean water and sanitation caused by the evisceration of USAID will lead to the deaths of about 4.5 million children under the age of five by 2030. 

The administration insists its policies will reduce wasteful spending, encourage work, promote parental rights, enforce immigration laws and return authority to the states. But wars are — and should be — measured by their casualties. Across an extraordinary range of administration policies, children, who are least able to protect themselves, are “collateral damage.” 

“Children are the world’s most valuable resource,” President John F. Kennedy proclaimed, “and its best hope for the future.” Apparently, the Trump administration does not agree. 

David Wippman is emeritus president of Hamilton College. Glenn C. Altschuler is the Thomas and Dorothy Litwin Emeritus Professor of American Studies at Cornell University.

data.title: Hunter Biden: 'I may have to' run for president in 2028
data.description:
Former President Biden’s (D) son, Hunter Biden, said that he may have to consider a 2028 presidential run amid speculation on who the Democratic nominee could be.

In a conversation with radio host John Catsimatidis, Biden was asked if had any plans to run for president where he said, “If I get your [Catsimatidis] endorsement, I may have to.”

When asked the same question earlier Biden stated, “I haven’t made up my mind.”

“The truth of the matter is that I think we have an incredible bench,” he said on “The Cats Roundtable,” mentioning Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D) and Illinois Governor JB Pritzker (D) before declaring “I love Gavin Newsom, personally.”

The governor of the nation’s most populous state has been open about his interest in seeking the top office. Newsom said in October 2025 that he would be “lying” if he said he wasn’t considering a bid for the White House after the 2026 midterms.

Other potential contenders include Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), former Vice President Kamala Harris and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.

Biden expressed during this interview that no matter who the candidate was, he wanted, “the next president to commit to one thing: to commit to adhering to the rule of law. To commit to the idea that we believe in this constitutional republic and the aspirations of normal Americans.”

“I truly, truly want whoever is our president to succeed. But particularly succeed in keeping this country safe. That’s their primary responsibility,” he said.

An Emerson College and The Hill survey that ranked potential match-ups between potential GOP and Democratic presidential candidates found Biden’s pick in a decent position.

Newsom held small leads over both potential Republican nominees, Vice President J.D. Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, unlike Ocasio-Cortez, who trailed both candidates. 

Biden added that what he cared about right now “is the 50 million Americans that are still suffering sick … with their addictions.”

While acknowledging his struggles with substance abuse issues, he noted in the interview that he recently celebrated seven and a half years of sobriety.

data.title: Ranking the Republican 2028 contenders
data.description:
President Trump dominates the political landscape, holding off lame-duck status for now.

But some signs are emerging that prominent members of his party are readying 2028 presidential bids. Those moves are only likely to accelerate after November’s midterms.

A post-Trump landscape will be tricky to navigate. The president has transformed his party during his decade in political life, shifting its policy positions on topics from immigration to trade, and transforming the tenor in which it conducts debate.

One big question for Republican primary voters in 2028 is whether they would prefer a nominee who tries to replicate Trump’s approach or one who seeks to write a new page.

There are plenty of options — assuming, of course, that Trump does not find a pretext to seek a third term. This is prohibited by any normal reading of the Constitution. Even Trump seems to — mostly — acknowledge it’s not possible.

Here are The Hill’s rankings:

1. Vice President Vance

Vice President Vance is the obvious heir apparent — as any vice president so much younger than the commander in chief would be.

Vance, 42, has always had a lot of backing within Trump’s inner circle, which helped him to be chosen as the president’s 2024 running mate in the first place.

Vance is also seen by the Make America Great Again (MAGA) grassroots as one of their own. 

This, admittedly, rather whitewashes Vance’s history, which includes once wondering to a friend if Trump could be “America’s Hitler.”

He has long disavowed his earlier criticism, however, and has been a loyal deputy to Trump. He is a fervent believer in the president’s right-wing populist message. 

Vance is also known to have been more skeptical than other senior figures in the administration about the decision to go to war in Iran. His perceived reluctance could be a political asset, given the unpopularity of the war with the public at large.

All of that being said, almost nobody believes Vance is a shoo-in for the nomination. It’s not clear Trump would endorse him. More broadly there are questions about Vance’s political skill while other critics see him as lacking in charisma. 

His showing in his only run for elected office was solid but unspectacular: He won a U.S. Senate seat representing his native Ohio by 7 points in 2022.

2. Secretary of State Marco Rubio

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vance are, by almost universal agreement, the two front-runners for the 2028 nomination.

In an Emerson College poll for The Hill last month, the secretary of State ran mostly better than Vance in hypothetical match-ups against several potential Democratic nominees.

Rubio has been in the national spotlight since 2010 when he won a U.S. Senate seat representing Florida. 

His experience has made him a more fluent political performer than Vance. Earlier this year, when each man took a turn at the lectern of the White House briefing room during then-press secretary Karoline Leavitt’s maternity leave, Rubio appeared to earn more praise.

The son of Cuban immigrants, Rubio is known for his longstanding desire to remove the regime that has been in place on the island since the late Fidel Castro led his revolutionary forces to victory in 1959. 

Rubio was enthused about the U.S. operation that seized Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro at the start of this year, and he has similarly hawkish views on Iran.

As such, he could position himself as something of a bridge between Trump’s “America First” supporters and the GOP’s more traditional wing on foreign affairs.

There are, however, questions of authenticity that have long floated around Rubio. 

He was also a harsh critic of Trump when he ran against him for the 2016 GOP nomination. The campaign may seem like ancient history now, but it would be excavated for attack ads by rival candidates if Rubio went forward with a 2028 bid.

3. Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas)

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) is one of the few figures outside Trump’s inner circle who could pose a real threat to Vance and Rubio. He is making little secret of the fact that he will probably try.

In a recent interview with MS NOW, Cruz pushed back against the idea that the GOP was beginning to coalesce around Vance as its likely nominee. 

When it came to the question of where the Republican Party was going and what its identity should be, Cruz stated that he would be “part of the discussion.”

Cruz, 55, is vigorously conservative, and his base in Texas gives him strong relationships with many big GOP donors.

Like Rubio, Cruz ran against Trump in 2016 before going on to make his peace with the president.

Even so, he can sometimes at least hint at criticism. In the MS NOW interview, he lauded Trump as a an “extraordinary” and “ferocious” figure but added: “I wish sometimes there was more message discipline and focus.”

Plenty of Republicans feel the same way. A Cruz campaign would be an intriguing test of how many of them the Texas senator could convert into supporters.

4. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis

Among serious contenders, few divide opinion as much as Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis.

His advocates point to his electoral successes in Florida, his embrace of the president’s agenda especially in terms of immigration and opposition to supposed “wokeness,” and the clout that comes from being governor of a large, increasingly Republican state.

But DeSantis’s downsides are equally obvious. His 2024 campaign against Trump never fired on all cylinders. It did, however, mark the Florida governor as a figure of suspicion in the minds of many Trump supporters.

While Vance, Rubio and Cruz are all assumed to be likely to run in 2028, that is less true of DeSantis, for whom the 2024 campaign was a bruising experience.

5. Donald Trump Jr.

Could the ardor that the GOP base feels for the current president be transferred to his eldest son?

It’s possible, but far from guaranteed.

The younger Trump has never run for office. Then again, neither had his father prior to 2016.

The bigger challenges would be twofold. 

First, the younger Trump makes news these days primarily because of business interests that have been deeply controversial. The sums of money involved are often vast. 

To take just one example, in July The Washington Post reported that “a portfolio of defense technology start-ups” in which Trump Jr. and his brother Eric Trump have invested “have collectively generated at least $3.2 billion in direct government business.”

Second, many doubt whether the force of his last name alone could propel Trump Jr. — a somewhat socially awkward figure not known for achievements outside the family — to the same political heights as his father.

6. Tucker Carlson

One of the most intriguing — and controversial — prospects within the GOP is the idea of a presidential run by the conservative commentator.

Tucker Carlson, who was once a staunch backer of Trump, has turned against him, primarily over the war in Iran. The former Fox News host has also become a fervent critic of Israel and its influence on American foreign policy.

To his fans, Carlson has remained true to the populist, “America First” ideology that they believe Trump was supposed to represent. To his detractors, he is stoking his own notoriety by attacking the president and giving a platform to fringe extremists.

Carlson has suggested he won’t run for president, but a livestream last month in which he outlined a 10-point manifesto hardly tamped down the speculation. 

He has also become strongly critical of the GOP itself, which appears to make a third-party bid more likely than a tilt at the Republican nomination.

7. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth

Late last month, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth emphatically denied an NBC News report that he had “told close friends and associates that he is considering a run for president in 2028.”

The secretary of Defense wrote on social media that the story was “100% false.”

Beyond the specifics of that story, a 2028 run doesn’t seem beyond the bounds of possibility for the ambitious former TV host.

But his tenure at the Pentagon has been deeply controversial, even among some Republicans.  

The recent departure of Army Secretary Dan Driscoll was one more data point fueling skepticism about Hegseth’s overall approach.

8. Sen. Tom Cotton (Ark.)

Sen. Tom Cotton’s (R-Ark.) appeal is somewhat similar to that of Cruz, except the Arkansas senator is a few years younger and unencumbered by the baggage of a previous run for the presidency.

Cotton, 49, is just as firmly conservative and a good communicator who keeps his profile high with regular appearances in friendly media.

Cotton faces the perennial problem for candidates who are seen as outside the top tier, however.

It’s hard to see him outflanking everyone to actually become the nominee, though it’s quite easy to see him as a possible vice presidential pick.

9. Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders

Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders still has a reservoir of support among Trump fans because of her stint as White House press secretary during his first term. 

She won election as governor of her native Arkansas in 2022 and is up for reelection this year. One recent poll had her leading only by a surprisingly narrow 5-point margin, but it would be a huge shock if she were to lose.

Sanders hasn’t said much about a possible 2028 bid, though she does have a book coming out this fall, which will see her step more firmly into the national spotlight.

Right now, she appears to be the only viable female candidate for the GOP nomination in 2028.

10. Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp

As a two-term governor of a large Southern state, Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp looks good on paper. He will soon have time on his hands to focus on a presidential bid as well: Term limits prevent him from seeking reelection this year.

The big problem for Kemp is his complicated and sometimes rancorous relationship with Trump.

For Kemp to become the nominee, the GOP would have to be ready to rebuke Trump and Trumpism. There is vanishingly little evidence that it is.

data.title: Russia calls talks with US envoys "useful"
data.description:
A Russian aide said talks between Russian President Vladimir Putin and two United States envoys were “highly useful” as the Americans attempt to restart stalled peace negotiations between Russia and Ukraine.

Yuri Ushakov, a foreign-policy adviser to Putin, said that U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner “outlined a number of ideas regarding possible avenues for a settlement” but declined to share details on these plans, according to Reuters. 

“The talks went beyond a mere exchange of views on resolving the Ukrainian crisis. Economic issues and ​potential major, mutually beneficial Russian-American projects were discussed in some detail,” Ushakov said.

The closed-door meeting – which lasted for over three hours – followed Putin authorizing a 72-hour pause on strikes against Kyiv to allow for the U.S. envoys’ safe travel, according to Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov. 

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky similarly said that after speaking with Witkoff and Kushner, the country was “ready to observe a ceasefire in airstrikes” in cities where negotiations were taking place. He added the pause in strikes would start now with a planned end on Monday.

This weekend marks the first time traveling to Kyiv for negotiations for both envoys.

President Trump has remained optimistic about the meetings, telling reporters in the Oval Office Friday the two men are “bringing with them a proposal to end the war,” though he did not elaborate on what the plan entailed.

The yearslong dispute between Russia and Ukraine intensified following the last U.S.-facilitated meetings in February. Moscow has initiated near-continuous attacks in and around Kyiv for over a week, hitting buildings, warehouses and the central headquarters for Ukraine’s security service.

Zelensky reported that ahead of the U.S. envoys’ visit, two airports located 300 miles east of Kyiv were also hit by Russian airstrikes – killing four people and injuring five others.

Ukraine hit back throughout August with long-range attacks on oil storage and refining facilities in Russia including strikes on logistics hubs of online retailer Wildberries which has unsettled Russians living far from the front and hurt small businesses.

data.title: Angie Craig throws hat in the ring for WNBA commissioner
data.description:
Rep. Angie Craig (D-Minn) offered herself up to replace retiring WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert, who recently announced her retirement amid the league’s growing popularity and recent controversies.

“Hey, @WNBA, I’m a free agent in January,” Rep. Craig wrote on social platform X Friday.

Craig lost to Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan in the Democratic primary for retiring Sen. Tina Smith’s (D-Minn.) seat, in what was considered a win for progressives over moderates within the party.

She has been an avid supporter of her state’s WNBA team, the Minnesota Lynx, and even wagered with Rep. Dan Goldman (D-N.Y.) about the outcome of the 2024 finals between the Lynx and the New York Liberty, but did not follow through on the bet in protest of a controversial call in the game

Her post responded to Engelbert’s retirement announcement after seven seasons leading the league. Under Engelbert’s tenure, the WNBA has grown from 12 teams to 15, with plans to expand to 18 by 2030, with recent seasons smashing viewership and attendance records.

However, Engelbert has also been criticized for discussions regarding transgender athletes, an issue which has become a major one for Republican lawmakers. She called it a complex and nuanced issue, saying in a memo that the league would continue discussions on the topic.

The conversation stemmed from comments made by Sophie Cunningham, a player for the Indiana Fever and teammate of superstar Caitlin Clark, who stated her priority was to advocate for, “young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn’t have to go against biological men.”

Craig, who was the first lesbian mother elected to Congress and a co-chair of the LGBT Equality Caucus, has opposed similar efforts in Congress, denouncing the “Protect Women’s Sports Act” that would have rewritten Title IX to define sex as “reproductive biology and genetics at birth.”

“Plain and simple, the Protect Women’s Sports Act is transphobic — and this type of discrimination has no place in the halls of Congress,” she said in 2020. “I am proud to do so today by emphatically denouncing this narrow-minded and hateful legislation.”

data.title: Trump admin ends $45M support for Namibia HIV program
data.description:
The Trump administration announced it will be ending $45 million in support for Namibia’s HIV response program following two decades of annual payments.

The U.S. will provide its final $45 million payment in the 2027 fiscal year as “this support will transition into a technical cooperation model,” according to a Friday joint statement from Namibia’s Ministry of International Relations & Trade and the U.S. Embassy in Namibia.

“This transition is a celebration of Namibia’s leadership and a model for what is possible,” U.S. Ambassador to Namibia John Giordano said in the statement.

Namibia will now integrate its HIV response into a “sustainable national health system” that is “guided by Namibia’s priorities, policies and legal frameworks.” 

The U.S.-backed program previously supported “investments in HIV testing, counselling, community-based organizations and other key health system intervention.”

The joint U.S.-Namibian effort notably surpassed global targets for HIV testing, treatment and viral suppression during its tenure, reporting that 97 percent of infants born to HIV-positive mothers tested negative for the disease. 

“As we evolve this partnership, we remain committed to a cooperation model that respects Namibia’s sovereignty and the integrity of our national health data,” said Dr. Esperance Luvindao, the Namibian Health minister.

The decision follows Namibia’s rejection of provisions that would have required the country to share sensitive health data with the U.S.,

According to The Namibian, the end of funding follows Namibia rejecting U.S. efforts to require the country to share sensitive health data as part of continued U.S. support.

Officials told the outlet that, “the Namibian government has made it unequivocally clear that the data-sharing or specimen-sharing agreements in their proposed forms are not in compliance with Namibia’s national laws.”

A report by the Kaiser Family Foundation and the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) found that global HIV response plunged in 2025 blaming a steep decline in U.S. support. 

The Trump administration previously created the “America First Global Health Strategy” that called for significant scale-down in U.S. funding for countries in the future, including global health programs which it called “inefficient and wasteful and created a culture of dependency among recipient countries.”

Other changes made by the administration include freezing and ultimately canceling global HIV projects, eliminating the U.S. Agency for International Development and canceling support to UNAIDS in 2025.

data.title: Trump's MAGA Inc. super-PAC funnels $10 million into Ken Paxton's Senate campaign
data.description:
President Trump’s super-PAC MAGA Inc. gave $10 million to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s (R) Senate campaign ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings published Saturday.

The $10 million payment, given to political media company, Del Ray Media, funded two attack ads against his Democratic opponent James Talarico — who is running a surprisingly competitive race in the historically red Lone Star State. 

A MAGA Inc. spokesperson, Alex Pfeiffer, told The Hill the MAGA Inc.-funded ads focus on how “High Tax Talarico” is planning to “take money out of Texans’ pockets.”

“MAGA Inc. is going to ensure Texas knows about Talarico’s radical policies and elects Ken Paxton to the U.S. Senate,” Pfeiffer said in her Saturday statement.

Talarico has made promises to put a higher tax on billionaires while cutting taxes for working families and small businesses, while Paxton has advocated for tax breaks and tackling the ongoing affordability crisis. 

The Lone Star Liberty PAC is slated to run similar attack ads against Talarico in September for being sympathetic to China, as the current state representative voted against legislation last year establishing criminal penalties for foreign entities purchasing Texas land.

The spending comes after Republican strategist Karl Rove said Wednesday that the “time is running out” for Paxton, who some polls have placed behind his opponent.

 “Of the president wants to have Paxton win, he needs to be tossing a lot of money Paxton’s way so that ads can be run that depict Talarico as the far-left winger that he is,” Rove said.

Trump said yesterday the PAC has $1 billion at its disposal amid Republicans’ calls for him to invest further in midterm candidates, though reports from June estimated its finances at around $400 million. He added that MAGA Inc. plans to spend between $400 and $500 million for November’s midterms, saving the rest for the 2028 election cycle.

Paxton pulled ahead in the Republican primary when he earned the president’s endorsement, though he has struggled to build a sustainable lead over his opponent since the primaries

Despite Trump winning the Lone Star state by around 14 points in the 2024 presidential election, Paxton trailed Talarico by 6-points in an August poll from Texas Public Opinion Research. 

The Republican has also faced several notable scandals, including the Texas state House voting to impeach him on corruption charges — of which the state senate later acquitted him.

Democrats are increasingly hopeful they can flip Texas’ seat, which Republicans have held for the last three decades. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report also shifted the Texas Senate race to a toss-up — citing Paxton’s high disapproval ratings and “notably underperforming even a generic Republican in GOP polling.”
